after.worked_solution:
Let's rewrite our integral as

$$
\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+3}}\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{{(\frac{x}{\sqrt{3}})}^{2}+1}}\,\text{d}x
$$

This integral resembles the basic integral for the inverse hyperbolic sine,

$$
\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{{u}^{2}+1}}\,\text{d}u=\operatorname{arsinh}⁡u+C.
$$

The only difference is that instead of ${u}^{2}$ as the variable, we have ${(\frac{x}{\sqrt{3}})}^{2}.$

So, let's substitute $u=\frac{x}{\sqrt{3}}.$ Differentiating, we get 

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\sqrt{3}\,\text{d}u.
$$

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and compute it, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+3}}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{{(\frac{x}{\sqrt{3}})}^{2}+1}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{{u}^{2}+1}}\cdot \sqrt{3}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\int \frac{\text{d}u}{\sqrt{{u}^{2}+1}} \\  & =\operatorname{arsinh}⁡u+C \\  & =\operatorname{arsinh}⁡(\frac{x}{\sqrt{3}})+C\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

content.knowledge_point: Calculating Indefinite Integrals Using Substitution With Inverse Hyperbolic Sine
content.worked_solution:
Let's rewrite our integral as

$$
\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+3}}\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{{(\frac{x}{\sqrt{3}})}^{2}+1}}\,\text{d}x
$$

This integral resembles the basic integral for the inverse hyperbolic sine,

$$
\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{{u}^{2}+1}}\,\text{d}u=\operatorname{arsinh}⁡u+C.
$$

The only difference is that instead of ${u}^{2}$ as the variable, we have ${(\frac{x}{\sqrt{3}})}^{2}.$

So, let's substitute $u=\frac{x}{\sqrt{3}}.$ Differentiating, we get 

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\sqrt{3}\,\text{d}u.
$$

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and compute it, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}+3}}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{{(\frac{x}{\sqrt{3}})}^{2}+1}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{{u}^{2}+1}}\cdot \sqrt{3}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\int \frac{\text{d}u}{\sqrt{{u}^{2}+1}} \\  & =\operatorname{arsinh}⁡u+C \\  & =\operatorname{arsinh}⁡(\frac{x}{\sqrt{3}})+C\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

content.worked_solution:
This integral resembles the basic integral for the inverse hyperbolic sine,

$$
\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{{u}^{2}+1}}\,\text{d}u=\operatorname{arsinh}⁡u+C.
$$

The only difference is that instead of ${u}^{2}$ as the variable, we have ${e}^{4x}={({e}^{2x})}^{2}.$

So, let's substitute $u={e}^{2x}.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=2{e}^{2x}\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{2{e}^{2x}}\,\text{d}u.
$$

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and compute it, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int \frac{2{e}^{2x}}{\sqrt{{e}^{4x}+1}}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{2{e}^{2x}}{\sqrt{{({e}^{2x})}^{2}+1}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int \frac{2u}{\sqrt{{u}^{2}+1}}\,\cdot (\frac{1}{2u}\,\text{d}u) \\  & =\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{{u}^{2}+1}}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\operatorname{arsinh}⁡u+C \\  & =\operatorname{arsinh}⁡{e}^{2x}+C\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{{u}^{2}+1}}\,\text{d}u=\operatorname{arsinh}⁡u+C.

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=6\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{6}\,\text{d}u.
$$

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and compute it, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int \frac{3}{\sqrt{36{x}^{2}+1}}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{3}{\sqrt{(6x)^{2}+1}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int \frac{3}{\sqrt{{u}^{2}+1}}\,\cdot (\frac{1}{6}\,\text{d}u) \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{{u}^{2}+1}}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{arsinh}⁡u+C \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\operatorname{arsinh}⁡6x+C\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

after.worked_solution:
This integral resembles the basic integral for the inverse hyperbolic sine,

$$
\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{{u}^{2}+1}}\,\text{d}u=\operatorname{arsinh}⁡u+C.
$$

The only difference is that instead of ${u}^{2}$ as the variable, we have ${e}^{2x}={({e}^{x})}^{2}.$

So, let's substitute $u={e}^{x}.$ Differentiating, we get

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}={e}^{x}\,⟹\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{{e}^{x}}\,\text{d}u.
$$

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and compute it, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int \frac{{e}^{x}}{\sqrt{{e}^{2x}+1}}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{{e}^{x}}{\sqrt{{({e}^{x})}^{2}+1}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int \frac{u}{\sqrt{{u}^{2}+1}}\,\cdot (\frac{1}{u}\,\text{d}u) \\  & =\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{{u}^{2}+1}}\,\text{d}u \\  & =\operatorname{arsinh}⁡u+C \\  & =\operatorname{arsinh}⁡{e}^{x}+C\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}-25}}\,\text{d}x=\frac{1}{5}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{{(\frac{x}{5})}^{2}-1}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

This integral resembles the basic integral for the inverse hyperbolic cosine,

$$
\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{{u}^{2}-1}}\,\text{d}u=\operatorname{arcosh}⁡u+C.
$$

The only difference is that instead of ${u}^{2}$ as the variable, we have ${(\frac{x}{5})}^{2}.$

So, let's substitute $u=\frac{x}{5}.$ Differentiating, we get 

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{5}\,⟹\,\text{d}x=5\,\text{d}u.
$$

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate it, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}-25}}\,\text{d}x & =\frac{1}{5}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{{(\frac{x}{5})}^{2}-1}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{1}{5}\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{{u}^{2}-1}}\cdot 5\,\text{d}u \\  & =\int \frac{\text{d}u}{\sqrt{{u}^{2}-1}} \\  & =\operatorname{arcosh}⁡u+C \\  & =\operatorname{arcosh}⁡(\frac{x}{5})+C\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$

after.worked_solution:
Let's rewrite our integral as

$$
\int \frac{7}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}-49}}\,\text{d}x=\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{{(\frac{x}{7})}^{2}-1}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

This integral resembles the basic integral for the inverse hyperbolic cosine,

$$
\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{{u}^{2}-1}}\,\text{d}u=\operatorname{arcosh}⁡u+C.
$$

The only difference is that instead of ${u}^{2}$ as the variable, we have ${(\frac{x}{7})}^{2}.$

So, let's substitute $u=\frac{x}{7}.$ Differentiating, we get 

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{7}\,⟹\,\text{d}x=7\,\text{d}u.
$$

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate it, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{7}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}-49}}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{{(\frac{x}{7})}^{2}-1}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{{u}^{2}-1}}\cdot 7\,\text{d}u \\  & =7\int \frac{\text{d}u}{\sqrt{{u}^{2}-1}} \\  & =7\operatorname{arcosh}⁡u+C \\  & =7\operatorname{arcosh}⁡(\frac{x}{7})+C\end{aligned}
$$

content.knowledge_point: Calculating Indefinite Integrals Using Substitution With Inverse Hyperbolic Cosine
content.worked_solution:
Let's rewrite our integral as

$$
\int \frac{7}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}-49}}\,\text{d}x=\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{{(\frac{x}{7})}^{2}-1}}\,\text{d}x.
$$

This integral resembles the basic integral for the inverse hyperbolic cosine,

$$
\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{{u}^{2}-1}}\,\text{d}u=\operatorname{arcosh}⁡u+C.
$$

The only difference is that instead of ${u}^{2}$ as the variable, we have ${(\frac{x}{7})}^{2}.$

So, let's substitute $u=\frac{x}{7}.$ Differentiating, we get 

$$
\frac{\text{d}u}{\text{d}x}=\frac{1}{7}\,⟹\,\text{d}x=7\,\text{d}u.
$$

Using the above, we can write the integral in terms of $u$ and evaluate it, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{7}{\sqrt{{x}^{2}-49}}\,\text{d}x & =\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{{(\frac{x}{7})}^{2}-1}}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int \frac{1}{\sqrt{{u}^{2}-1}}\cdot 7\,\text{d}u \\  & =7\int \frac{\text{d}u}{\sqrt{{u}^{2}-1}} \\  & =7\operatorname{arcosh}⁡u+C \\  & =7\operatorname{arcosh}⁡(\frac{x}{7})+C\end{aligned}
$$
